clause_list.title: Quality Assurance and Quality Control
clause_list.text: Chapter 8 defines the contractual responsibilities for Quality Assurance (QA) and Quality Control (QC) in the design, manufacturing, and construction of latticed steel transmission structures.

clause_list.title: Introduction
clause_list.text: The contract between the purchaser and the supplier shall state the responsibilities of each party and the conditions under which the work will be accepted or rejected.

clause_list.title: Quality Assurance
clause_list.text: Quality assurance (QA) is the responsibility of the purchaser. The bid documents shall outline the QA methods, types of inspections, and records that will be required to determine the acceptability of the product at each stage of the design, manufacturing, and construction process.

clause_list.title: Quality Control
clause_list.text: Quality control (QC) is the responsibility of the supplier. The supplier shall have a QC program consisting of a written document or a series of departmental memoranda that establishes the procedures and methods of operation that affect the quality of the work.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Loading, Geometry, and Analysis
clause_list.section: Commentary — C2.0 Loading, Geometry, and Analysis
clause_list.text: Commentary C2 provides explanatory background on design-factored loads, structure geometry classifications, plan bracing/diaphragm placement, and structural analysis methods (first-order, second-order P-Delta, tension-only, post-buckling, and equivalent beam mast models).

clause_list.title: Commentary: Introduction (Load Factors)
clause_list.section: Commentary — C2.0 Loading, Geometry, and Analysis
clause_list.text: Design-factored loads are loads multiplied by load factors. The overload capacity factors specified by the National Electrical Safety Code (IEEE 2012) are load factors according to the terminology of this Standard.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Loads, Climbing & Fall Protection
clause_list.section: Commentary — C2.0 Loading, Geometry, and Analysis
clause_list.text:
Extensive background information on the selection of design-factored loads can be found in Guidelines for Electrical Transmission Line Structural Loading (ASCE MOP 74, 2009) and the National Electrical Safety Code (IEEE 2012).
Minimum legislated loads are specified in applicable codes covered by state and local authorities. Local climatic conditions may dictate loads in excess of legislated loads (wind, ice, or both combined at a specified temperature). Line security (measures to prevent progressive/cascading line failure) is often handled by specifying one or more longitudinal load conditions. Construction and maintenance loads should also be specified.
It is suggested that tower members used to support maintenance personnel when climbing a tower be capable of supporting a vertical worker load as defined in ASCE MOP 74 (2009) applied independently of all other loads without permanent distortion of the member. If end connection assembly bolts are properly tightened, the frictional restraining effect may be considered.
If fall protection is required, the purchaser should provide the EOR with all climbing requirements in accordance with IEEE 1307 (2004) or OSHA specifications.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Geometric Configurations & Diaphragm Spacing
clause_list.section: Commentary — C2.0 Loading, Geometry, and Analysis
clause_list.text:
Three basic structure definitions are recommended: suspension, strain, and dead-end structures. The term 'tangent' is prefixed for zero line angle, and 'angle' is used when there is a line angle (tangent suspension, angle suspension, tangent strain, angle strain, tangent dead-end, and angle dead-end).
Guyed structures rely on internal or external guy cables for stability and are normally less rigid than self-supporting structures.
In most structures, horizontal bracing in the face of the tower, with an internal diaphragm, is required to provide adequate rigidity and to distribute shear and torsional forces. It is normally used at levels where there is a change in the slope of the structure leg, and in square/rectangular structures to support horizontal struts and reduce distortion under torsional or oblique wind loads. Recommended locations for plan bracing with or without a diaphragm are shown in Fig. C2-1 (Table C2-1). For structures taller than 200 ft (61 m), or heavy dead-end towers, it is suggested that horizontal bracing with a diaphragm be installed at intervals not exceeding 75 ft (23 m).

clause_list.title: Commentary: Methods of Analysis
clause_list.section: Commentary — C2.0 Loading, Geometry, and Analysis
clause_list.text:
A lattice structure is described by a one-line design drawing (Fig. C2-2) and analyzed as an ideal elastic 3D truss of straight members or cables pin-connected at joints (located at the intersections of member centroidal axes).
- First-order linear elastic truss analysis ignores secondary effects of the deflected structure, and forces in redundant members equal zero. Used for conventional, relatively rigid self-supporting structures.
- Second-order (geometrically nonlinear) elastic analysis includes P-Delta effects in the deformed configuration (Peyrot 1985) and is normally required for flexible self-supporting structures and guyed structures.
- Tension-only systems (Fig. C2-3) assume bracing members with L/r > 300 cannot resist compression.
- Post-buckling member behavior (Fig. C2-4): Method 1 assumes constant buckling load F_max beyond e_max; Method 2 assumes zero load after e_max; Method 3 models reduced capacity along a post-buckling performance curve (Prickett et al. 1989).
- If the included angle alpha between a bracing member and the supported member approaches 15 degrees, the supported member should be investigated for stability. Insufficiently stiff bracing (Fig. C2-5) can induce bending moments in leg or cross-arm chords, which should be modeled as beam elements with principal axes properly oriented.
- Dynamic seismic analysis is generally not needed for latticed towers (Long 1974).
- Guyed masts and latticed H-frame columns (Fig. C2-6) may be modeled as 3D trusses or equivalent beam elements.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Design of Members
clause_list.text: Commentary C3 provides background on steel grades up to 65 ksi, wind-induced member vibration limits, SSRC column formulas, single-angle effective length curves (Curves 1–6), partial joint restraint stiffness evaluation, cold-formed effective widths, lateral-torsional buckling of beams, and redundant member forces.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Introduction & Scope Limits
clause_list.text: This standard is suitable for steels with yield points up to 65 ksi (448 MPa) and for width-to-thickness values of 25 for projecting elements, such as angle legs and channel flanges. Higher values may be used where verified by tests, provided results are adjusted to the ASTM yield and tensile values of the material and nominal design dimensions.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Material (Fu/Fy Ratio)
clause_list.text: A ratio of Fu / Fy >= 1.15 is suggested for steel used for members.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Minimum Sizes (Weathering Steel)
clause_list.text: If weathering steel is to be used, consideration should be given to increasing the suggested minimum thickness.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Slenderness Ratios & Aeolian Vibration
clause_list.text:
Tension-only members (L/r >= 300) bow out-of-plane without permanent set when subjected to compression and return to their original position upon load removal.
Damaging vibration of steel members in latticed towers usually occurs at steady wind speeds less than 20 mi/h (32 km/h). Tests on shapes with L/r <= 250 show that the possibility of damaging vibration is minimal (Carpena and Diana 1971). Tension-hanger members are prone to vibration, but L/r values as large as 375 have been used successfully. In areas of steady winds over extended periods (mountain passes or flat plains), allowable L/r values may need to be reduced, and blocking the outstanding leg of angles at connections should be avoided.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Properties of Sections
clause_list.text: Procedures for computing the torsional constant J, the warping constant Cw, the shear center, and other section properties are given in Timoshenko and Gere (1961), Yu (1986), and the AISI Cold-Formed Steel Design Manual (2008). For cold-formed shapes with small inside-bend radii (2t), section properties can be determined on the basis of square corners without significant difference.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Design Compression (SSRC & Euler)
clause_list.text: The Structural Stability Research Council (SSRC) formula (originally developed in 1966) for the ultimate strength of centrally loaded columns in the inelastic range and the Euler formula in the elastic range are used in this Standard.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Compression Members: Angles
clause_list.text: A single angle in axial compression can fail by torsional-flexural buckling about the u-axis, by z-axis flexural buckling (Fig. C3-1), or by local buckling of the legs. Local buckling and purely torsional buckling are identical if the angle has equal legs and is simply supported and free to warp at each end; therefore, such members are customarily checked only for flexural and local buckling.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Determination of Fa (Local Buckling)
clause_list.text: The flat-width-to-thickness ratio w/t that enables the leg to reach yield stress without local buckling is set at 80 / sqrt(Fy) for Fy in ksi (210 / sqrt(Fy) for Fy in MPa). Unequal-leg angles are designed by establishing the design stress based on the w/t value of the long leg (Gaylord and Wilhoite 1985).

clause_list.title: Commentary: Effective Lengths & Partial Joint Restraint Evaluation
clause_list.text:
For angles in compression (other than leg members bolted in both faces where K = 1), eccentricity of the connection is the predominant factor in the lower L/r range (L/r <= 120), whereas rotational restraint becomes the predominant factor in the higher L/r range (L/r > 120). The transition point is taken as L/r = 120.
Fig. C3-2 plots the normalized compression curves (Curves 1 through 6 from ASCE Manual of Practice No. 52):
- Curve 1: Eq. (3.7-5), concentric both ends (0 <= L/r <= 120)
- Curve 2: Eq. (3.7-6), concentric one end, normal eccentricity other end (0 <= L/r <= 120)
- Curve 3: Eq. (3.7-7), normal framing eccentricities both ends (0 <= L/r <= 120)
- Curve 4: Eq. (3.7-8), unrestrained both ends (L/r >= 120)
- Curve 5: Eq. (3.7-9), partially restrained one end (L/r >= 120)
- Curve 6: Eq. (3.7-10), partially restrained both ends (L/r >= 120)
Normal framing eccentricity implies that the centroid of the bolt pattern is located between the heel of the angle and the centerline of the connected leg.
To justify using the partial rotational restraint values of KL/r in Eqs. (3.7-9), (3.7-10), (3.7-12), and (3.7-13), the following evaluation is suggested (see Fig. C3-3):
(a) The restrained member should be connected to the restraining member with at least two bolts;
(b) The restraining member should have a stiffness factor I/L in the stress plane (where I/L = r^2 * A / L = r * A / (L/r)) that equals or exceeds the sum of the stiffness factors in the stress plane of the restrained members connected to it; and
(c) Angle members connected solely to a gusset plate should not be considered to have end restraint against rotation.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Unsupported Length with Varying Forces
clause_list.text: The effective length factor K' for an unsupported length of a member with varying force magnitudes across subpanels (such as the tower body extension and K-bracing systems shown in Fig. C3-4) is determined using Eqs. (3.7-14a) and (3.7-14b) (Johnston 1988). The change in force at the subpanel point provides partial restraint for both rotation and translation.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Compression Members: Symmetrical Lipped Angles
clause_list.text: Lips increase the local buckling strength of angle legs, so torsional-flexural buckling must be checked using the equivalent radius of gyration rtf [Eq. (3.8-1)]. If the member is free to warp and rotate about the u-axis at each end, K = 1; if prevented at both ends, K = 0.5; if prevented at one end, K = 0.7. Mixed end conditions can be treated by replacing rt and ru in Eq. (3.8-1) with rt/Kt and ru/Ku, using Kt = 1 in Eq. (3.8-2) when computing adjusted KL/r values in Section 3.7.4.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Compression Members Not Covered in Sections 3.7 and 3.8
clause_list.text: Commentary C3.9 explains post-buckling effective width reductions (AISI S100-07), axis substitutions for singly/doubly symmetric sections in Eqs. (3.8-1) and (3.8-2), and upper/lower bound methods for nonsymmetric sections.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Maximum w/t Ratio & Postbuckling Strength
clause_list.text: Where element slenderness w/t is too large to develop uniform stress Fa over the full cross section, the postbuckling strength of elements that buckle prematurely is accounted for by using an effective width b that gives the same resultant force at uniform stress Fa.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Effective Widths of Elements in Compression
clause_list.text: Effective width formulas are derived from the North American Specification for the Design of Cold-Formed Steel Structural Members (AISI 2007). Effective widths are determined at design stress Fa based on the gross radius of gyration, while allowable force P is obtained by multiplying Fa by the reduced area. When applying Eqs. (3.8-1) and (3.8-2) to sections with x and y principal axes, the axis of symmetry (x or y) is substituted for u.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Nonsymmetric Cross Sections
clause_list.text: An analysis based on the elastic buckling stress of a nonsymmetric member (requiring the solution of a cubic equation, Zavelani and Faggiano 1985) gives an upper bound to the allowable value. A lower bound can be obtained by proportioning the member so that the maximum combined stress caused by axial load and moment equals the yield stress (Madugula and Ray 1984).

clause_list.title: Commentary: Tension Members
clause_list.text: Commentary C3.10 provides background on tension members and guy assemblies.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Guys
clause_list.text: The elastic limit of wire rope is approximately 65% of its breaking strength; therefore, 0.65 times minimum breaking strength is consistent with Fy for tension members. Guy tension calculations should account for anchor movement, guy length/size/modulus, and structure deflection. On tangent structures, pretensioning guys to 10% of rated breaking strength is normally sufficient to avoid a slack guy.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Axial Compression and Bending
clause_list.text: Equations (3.12-1) and (3.12-2) correspond to the AISC and AISI interaction formulas expressed in terms of force P and moment M. Values of Cm are given only for the non-sway case since lateral sidesway of one end relative to the other is not likely in latticed transmission towers.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Axial Tension and Bending
clause_list.text: In Eq. (3.13-1), Max and May are determined according to Section 3.14 so that lateral buckling of laterally unsupported members is accounted for even when axial force P is tensile. Eq. (3.13-1) matches AISC 360 (2010).

clause_list.title: Commentary: Beams
clause_list.text: Allowable compressive stresses for laterally unsupported beams in Section 3.14 are computed from the axial compression formulas (Section 3.6) through the use of an equivalent radius of gyration.

clause_list.title: Commentary: I, Channel, and Cruciform Sections
clause_list.text: Equation (3.14-1) takes both St. Venant torsional stiffness J and warping stiffness Cw into account, yielding more accurate lateral-torsional buckling stresses than simplified formulas that neglect either Cw or J (Clark and Hill 1960; Gaylord et al. 1992).

clause_list.title: Commentary: Singly Symmetric I and T Sections
clause_list.text: The approximate procedures for T sections and singly symmetric I sections in Section 3.14.6 give very good results.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Other Singly Symmetric Open Sections
clause_list.text: The formulas in Section 3.14.7 give identical results to those in the AISI (2008) specification; Example 17 in Appendix B illustrates the calculation of the section property j.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Equal Leg Angles in Bending
clause_list.text:
The formulas in Section 3.14.8 give critical moments for pure bending (constant moment) of equal leg angles and are conservative for moment gradients, but do not account for twist if the load does not act through the shear center (Leigh et al. 1984; Madugula and Kennedy 1985).
If the formulas are used for relatively thin angles with b/t larger than 16, it is suggested that the resulting allowable moments be reduced by 10% if the member is not to be tested.
Deflections may be computed as the resultant of the u- and z-axis deflection components; there are no established limits of deflection for beams in transmission tower applications.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Design Shear
clause_list.text: Commentary C3.15 explains the web slenderness and shear stress limits for beam webs.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Beam Webs in Shear
clause_list.text: The limiting web depth-to-thickness ratio h/t <= 200 matches the AISI (2008) specification limit for Fy = 60 ksi (413 MPa) and is adequate for steels with Fy <= 60 ksi. The design shear stresses match the AISC and AISI specifications multiplied by their respective factors of safety.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Redundant Members
clause_list.text: Redundant members provide intermediate support for stressed primary members. Common design practice is to design redundant members for 1.5% to 2.5% of the load in the supported member.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Welded Angles
clause_list.text: Welded angles are seldom used but are sometimes necessary for large single-angle members (e.g., greater than 8 in. x 8 in. or odd-size angles). Welded angles should be fabricated using steel that is suitable for welding and galvanizing.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Design of Connections
clause_list.text: Commentary C4 provides engineering background and test data for bolted connections, fastener shear/tension/combined capacities, bearing stresses, punching thickness limits, Table C4-1 minimum distances, oversized attachment holes, and post angle butt/lap splices.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Introduction (Tolerances & Nut Locking)
clause_list.text: The detailer should provide for normal rolling tolerances (ASTM A6) to avoid underrun of edge distances. Bolts (ASTM A394) are installed to the snug-tight condition or a specified minimum torque; locking devices (such as Palnuts or lock washers) are used by many utilities to minimize nut loosening caused by vibration or joint flexure.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Fasteners
clause_list.text: Commentary C4.3 covers bolt shear capacity, bolt tension capacity, and combined shear and tension interaction.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Bolt Shear Capacity
clause_list.text: Because tower bolts are installed to the snug-tight condition or a specified minimum torque, load transfer across a bolt is governed by direct shear rather than friction. ASTM A394 provides specified minimum shear values with threads included in or excluded from the shear plane. The design shear stress of 0.62 * Fu for other bolts is conservative (Kulak et al. 1988).

clause_list.title: Commentary: Bolt Tension Capacity
clause_list.text: The ASTM proof-load stress is approximately equal to the bolt yield stress, and 0.6 * Fu is a conservative estimate when proof load is not specified. Exceeding the yield stress causes permanent stretch in the bolt, which can loosen the nut and cause loss of tightness in the joint.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Bolts Subject to Combined Shear and Tension
clause_list.text: Tests on fasteners indicate that the interaction between shear and tension is represented by an ellipse (Higgins and Munse 1952; Chesson et al. 1965; Kulak et al. 1988) with major and minor axes based on the design shear and tension capacities.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Design Bearing Stress
clause_list.text:
Designs produced with bearing stresses <= 1.5 * Fu under factored loads have demonstrated satisfactory control over bolt-hole ovalization during full-scale tower tests.
The design bearing value on the bolts should also be checked if the tensile strength Fu of the member material exceeds the Fu value of the bolt—for example, when an ASTM A394 Type 0 bolt (Fu = 74 ksi [510 MPa]) connects ASTM A572 Grade 65 steel (Fu = 80 ksi [551 MPa]). In that case, the full bolt diameter is used with design bearing stress equal to 1.5 * Fu of the bolt (Wilhoite 1986).

clause_list.title: Commentary: Minimum Distances
clause_list.text: Commentary C4.5 explains the experimental basis for end distances, center-to-center bolt hole spacing, and edge distances, as illustrated in Fig. C4-1 and Table C4-1.

clause_list.title: Commentary: End Distance & Punching Thickness Guidelines
clause_list.text:
Eq. (4.5-1) provides the end distance required for strength (including a 1.2 factor for single-fastener connection uncertainties per Kulak et al. 1988). Eq. (4.5-2) (1.3d for stressed members; 1.2d in Eq. 4.5-4 for redundant members) is a practical lower bound. Eq. (4.5-3) (t + d/2) prevents hole breakout during punching of thick members and is not required when holes are drilled.
The following maximum punching thickness guidelines have been used satisfactorily:
- For 36 ksi (248 MPa) yield steel: material thickness t <= hole diameter;
- For 50 ksi (345 MPa) yield steel: material thickness t <= hole diameter - 1/16 in. (1.6 mm); and
- For 65 ksi (448 MPa) yield steel: material thickness t <= hole diameter - 1/8 in. (3.2 mm).
Fig. C4-1 and Table C4-1 illustrate the governing end, edge, and center-to-center distances for a 3/4-in. A394 Type 0 bolt in A36 steel. Fig. C4-2 shows how e_min is measured when a member end is clipped at an angle.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Center-to-Center Bolt Hole Spacing
clause_list.text: Eq. (4.5-5) is the strength expression for end distance [Eq. (4.5-1)] plus 0.6d (used instead of 0.5d to control material reduction from hole breakout during punching). For low bearing values, installation wrench clearance may govern: convenient erection spacing is determined by adding 3/8 in. (9.5 mm) to the width across the points of the nut being used (see Table C4-1).

clause_list.title: Commentary: Edge Distance
clause_list.text: Tests by Bodegom et al. (1984) established the ratio 0.85 between required rolled edge distance and required end distance [Eq. (4.5-6)]. When the edge distance is to a sheared or mechanically guided flame-cut edge, 1/16 in. (1.6 mm) is added [Eq. (4.5-7)].

clause_list.title: Commentary: Attachment Holes & Everyday Loading Wear Limit
clause_list.text:
Oversized attachment holes (dh <= 2d, Fig. C4-3) are commonly used for insulator strings, overhead ground wires, and guys, and are not used where connections experience load reversal. Eq. (4.6-1) was developed by replacing e in Eq. (4.5-1) with (L - 0.5 * dh), solving for P, and multiplying by 0.9. The dimension L perpendicular to the line of action of P may be reduced if analysis shows that the sum of tensile stress P/A and tensile bending stress does not exceed 0.67 * Fy.
Eq. (4.6-2) limits the bearing stress to 0.9 times the design value for standard holes (1.35 * d * t * Fu) to provide an additional factor for wear.
For everyday loading (bare weight of conductor at 60°F [16°C] final sag, plus steady prevailing wind where applicable), P should not exceed 0.5 * d * t * Fu to avoid indentation and excessive wear under sustained loading.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Post Angle Member Splices (Butt vs. Lap)
Commentary: Detailing and Fabrication
clause_list.text: Commentary C5 provides supplementary guidance on fabrication and welding of built-up angles.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Fabrication
clause_list.text: See Section C5.2.5.2 for fabrication and straightening requirements for welded angles.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Welding
clause_list.text: See Section C5.2.5.2 for complete and partial penetration groove weld requirements on welded angles.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Welded Angles Fabrication
clause_list.text: Normally, welded angles should be fabricated using complete penetration groove welds conforming to AWS D1.1 (2010). Plate edges forming the toes should be smooth, straight, and deburred, with shape tolerances conforming at minimum to ASTM A6 (2014). All welded angles should be mechanically straightened before galvanizing, and the EOR should specify if stress relieving is required. If partial weld penetration is used, the requirements of Section 3.17 apply.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Testing
clause_list.text: Commentary C6 provides practical guidance on full-scale prototype proof testing, test foundations (rigid vs. direct-embedded), material overstrength limits (Fig. C6-1), strain gauging, rigging/insulator simulation, and load/deflection measurement accuracy.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Introduction to Proof Testing
clause_list.text: A proof test is performed on a full-size prototype structure or component under static design-factored loads on ideal foundations to verify stress distribution, member and connection adequacy, and fit-up before quantity production.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Foundations for Prototype Testing
clause_list.text: Commentary C6.2 covers test foundation requirements for rigid structures, direct embedded structures, and individual components.

clause_list.title: Commentary: General Test Foundation Reactions
clause_list.text: The type, rigidity, strengths, and moment reactions of the actual attachments of a prototype to a test bed have a major effect on the ability of the prototype members to resist the applied loads; consequently, the reactions of the test foundations should be similar to the expected reactions of the in-service foundations.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Rigid Structures
clause_list.text: Tests of a fairly rigid, four-legged, latticed structure designed for stub angles set in concrete, anchor bolts and base plates on concrete, or earth grillage foundations, are usually performed on special stub angles bolted or welded to the test station's rigid base. Accurate positioning of the footings is necessary to prevent abnormal stresses in the structure members.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Direct Embedded Structures
clause_list.text: It is recommended that structures designed for direct embedment be tested in a two-part program (Sections C6.2.3.1 and C6.2.3.2).

clause_list.title: Commentary: Embedded Portion
clause_list.text: Soil properties at a permanent test station probably do not match the properties of the soil on the transmission line. Tests that are dependent on soil resistance should be done at the line site, since only load cases that control the anchorage design need to be performed.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Aboveground Portion
clause_list.text: The aboveground portion of the prototype should be modified to be bolted or welded to the test station's foundation. All controlling load cases should be applied to this prototype.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Component Testing
clause_list.text: For component tests, especially single members, the amount of rotational rigidity of the supports is critical. All other parameters of the attachments of the prototype to the test bed should also be as close to the in-service conditions as possible.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Prototype Material Overstrength Limits
clause_list.text: Actual yield points of tension members and of compression members with KL/r < 120 are critical in determining prototype member capacity. Fig. C6-1 provides suggested maximum actual yield points for prototype members as a function of specified minimum yield strength Fy (e.g., max actual yield ~47 ksi for Fy = 36 ksi; ~62 ksi for Fy = 50 ksi; ~76 ksi for Fy = 65 ksi). If specified steel is not used for these critical members in the test tower, design and detail drawings should be updated to reflect the grade used during the test.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Fabrication of Prototype
clause_list.text: Normally, the prototype is not galvanized for the test unless the purchaser's order states otherwise.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Strain Measurements
clause_list.text: Stress determination methods, primarily strain gauging, may be used to monitor the loads in individual members during testing. Comparison of the measured unit stress to the predicted unit stress is useful in validating the proof test and refining analysis methods.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Assembly and Erection Plumb Tolerance
clause_list.text: The erected prototype should conform with the special requirements of the purchaser's instructions; many purchasers specify both minimum torque for bolt tightening and that the vertical axis should not be out of plumb by more than 1 in. (25 mm) for every 40 ft (12 m) of height.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Load Application
clause_list.text: V-type insulator strings should be loaded at the point where the insulator strings intersect using articulated bars or wire rope slings. Compression on unbraced panels caused by bridling of load lines should be avoided. As a structure deflects under load, load lines may change their direction of pull; adjustments should be made in the applied loads or the test rigging should be offset accordingly so that vertical, transverse, and longitudinal vectors at the load points match the tower loading schedule.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Loading Procedure Sequence
clause_list.text: It is recommended that the primary consideration in establishing the sequence of testing should be that those load cases that have the least influence on the results of successive tests be tested first. A secondary consideration should be to simplify the operations necessary to carry out the test program.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Load Measurement Accuracy
clause_list.text: The effects of pulley friction should be minimized. Load measurement by monitoring the load in a single part of a multipart block and tackle arrangement should be avoided. Accuracy of load measurement should be within 2% of the applied load.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Deflections Accuracy
clause_list.text: Points to be monitored should be selected to verify the deflections predicted by the design analysis. Accuracy of deflection measurements should be within the greater of 1 in. (25 mm) or 5% of the total deflection.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Disposition of Prototype
clause_list.text: An undamaged structure is usually accepted for use in the transmission line after all components are visually inspected and found to be structurally sound and within tolerances.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Structural Members and Connections Used in Foundations
clause_list.text: Commentary C7 covers pressed plate washers, corrosive groundwater protection, ACI 349 concrete side-cover distances for tension bursting and shear blowout, pier tie reinforcement (Fig. C7-1), and stud/angle shear connectors.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Introduction to Foundation Steelwork
clause_list.text: The material in Chapter 7 covers structural members and connections normally supplied by the steel fabricators.

clause_list.title: Commentary: General Considerations
clause_list.text: See Section C7.2.2 for pressed plate foundation attachments.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Pressed Plates
clause_list.text: For the pressed plate foundation, a relatively thick steel plate washer is welded to the bottom of the stub angle. The plate washer allows an attachment for bolting to the pressed plate and provides a transfer of the axial load from the stub angle to the corners of the pressed plate.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Deterioration Considerations
clause_list.text: Concrete foundations should be properly sloped to drain so that water pockets do not accumulate with ground material and cause excessive corrosion of the tower base material. Where groundwater is highly corrosive (ash pits, industrial drainage areas, oil refineries), concrete foundations should be used, or steel members exposed to severe ground conditions should receive an additional protective coating (such as bitumastic compound) and be increased in thickness at least 1/16 in. (1.6 mm) as a corrosion allowance.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Concrete Side Cover & Pier Reinforcing (ACI 349)
clause_list.text:
ACI 349 (1985) anchorage requirements are modified using the yield strength Fy of the anchorage material to ensure ductile steel failure prior to brittle concrete failure:
- Eq. (C7.5-1) Side cover distance for tension to prevent lateral bursting for smooth anchor bolts: mt = 0.66 * d * sqrt(Fy / sqrt(f'c)) (with Fy and f'c in psi).
- Eq. (C7.5-2) Side cover distance for anchorage shear: ms = 1.8 * d * sqrt(Fy / sqrt(f'c)) (with Fy and f'c in psi), where the bolt diameter required for shear only may be used, but not less than ms/3 for actual d or 4 in.
Eqs. (C7.5-1) and (C7.5-2) can also be used for stub angles using an equivalent diameter based on the net section of the stub angle.
Horizontal ties and vertical pier reinforcing must intercept the assumed tension and shear failure cones as shown in Fig. C7-1 (Shipp and Haninger 1983).

clause_list.title: Commentary: Shear Connectors
clause_list.text: Commentary C7.6 provides references and assumptions for stud and angle shear connectors.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Stud Shear Connectors
clause_list.text: Additional information on stud shear connectors [Fig. 7-3(c)] is available in Salmon and Johnson (1990).

clause_list.title: Commentary: Angle Shear Connectors
clause_list.text: The values obtained using Eq. (7.6-2) [Fig. 7-3(b)] are based on initial yielding of the angle in bending at a stress of 1.19 * f'c in the concrete. The 1.19 constant is based on the concrete pier having an area at least four times as large as the bearing area of a pair of shear connector angles.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Quality Assurance and Quality Control
clause_list.section: Commentary — C8.0 Quality Assurance and Quality Control
clause_list.text: Commentary C8 outlines the interaction between the purchaser's QA program and the supplier's QC program.

clause_list.title: Commentary: QA/QC Introduction & Joint Review
clause_list.section: Commentary — C8.0 Quality Assurance and Quality Control
clause_list.text: A joint review of the QA and QC requirements and agreement by both the purchaser and the supplier allows for conflict resolution before ordering materials. Typical items discussed include acceptance of material specifications, sources of supply, material identification, storage, traceability procedures, and certified mill test reports.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Quality Assurance Scope
clause_list.section: Commentary — C8.0 Quality Assurance and Quality Control
clause_list.text: The purchaser's QA program defines the personnel responsible for contract performance, engineering review, shop inspection (material certification, material handling, cutting and piece mark identification, bending, welding, NDT, galvanizing, fit-up, and bundling for shipment), and receipt of material in the field.

clause_list.title: Commentary: Quality Control Scope
clause_list.section: Commentary — C8.0 Quality Assurance and Quality Control
clause_list.text: The supplier's QC program establishes quality control checks for planning and scheduling, engineering, drafting, purchasing, production, and shipping, ensuring that the finished product meets the purchaser's allowable tolerances.

clause_list.title: Appendix A: Notation
clause_list.text:
Symbols used in ASCE/SEI 10-15 (with Customary and SI units):
- A, Ag, An, As, Asc, At, Av = cross-sectional, gross, net, bolt tensile stress, stud shear connector, net tension, and net shear areas (in.^2) (mm^2)
- a = distance from shear center to load plane (in.) (mm)
- b, b1, b2 = effective design widths of elements, or width of leg - t/2 (in.) (mm)
- C, Cb, Cc, Cm = stress gradient constant, bending moment coefficient, elastic/inelastic column slenderness limit, and beam-column interaction coefficient
- Cw = warping constant of cross section (in.^6) (mm^6)
- D = downthrust load on anchor bolts (kip) (N)
- d, dh = nominal bolt diameter or minimum lip depth, and attachment hole diameter (in.) (mm)
- E, Ec = modulus of elasticity of steel (29,000 ksi [200,000 MPa]) and concrete (ksi) (MPa)
- e, e_min, f, f_min, s, s_min, g = actual and required end distance, edge distance, longitudinal pitch, and transverse gauge (in.) (mm)
- Fa, Fb, Fcr, Ft, Ft(v), Fu, Fv, Fy = design axial compressive stress, design bending stress, local buckling critical stress, design tensile stress, combined shear/tension bolt stress, specified minimum tensile strength, design shear stress, and specified minimum yield stress (ksi) (MPa)
- f'c = specified compressive strength of concrete at 28 days (ksi) (MPa)
- I, Ips, Iu, Ix, Iy, Iz, J = moments of inertia and St. Venant torsional constant (in.^4) (mm^4)
- j = section property for torsional-flexural buckling (in.) (mm)
- K, Kt, Ku, Kx, Ky, K' = effective length factors
- L, Lu, Lx, Ly, Lz, L' = unbraced lengths (in.) (mm)
- Max, May, Mb, Me, Mx, My, Myc, Myt, M1, M2 = allowable, lateral buckling, elastic critical, applied, and yield bending moments (in.-kip) (mm-N)
- P, Pa, Pex, Pey, Pr, Qn, T, V, V1, V2 = member/connector forces and capacities (kip) (N)
- r, rps, rt, rtf, ru, rx, ry, rz = radii of gyration (in.) (mm)
- S, Sxc = elastic section moduli (in.^3) (mm^3)
- t, w, w' = element thickness, flat width of element, and flat width of edge stiffener (in.) (mm)
- uo, xo, yo = distances between shear center and centroid (in.) (mm)
- alpha, theta, mu, phi, Psi = bracing angle, lip/load angle, friction coefficient, resistance factor, and unit conversion factor

clause_list.title: Appendix B: Design Examples Overview
clause_list.text: Appendix B contains 17 worked engineering examples (Examples 1 through 17) illustrating the application of ASCE/SEI 10-15 to equal-leg angles, end connection restraint, double-angle struts, K-bracing, subdivided panels, X-brace systems with and without redundant supports, cold-formed plain and lipped angles, M-sections, channels, T-sections, 60-degree Schifflerized angles, and j-value determination.

clause_list.title: Example 1: Equal Leg Angle with Symmetrical Bracing
clause_list.text:
Evaluates tower leg angle capacity under symmetrical bracing (L/rz critical, concentric loading per Eq. 3.7-4):
1. L8 x 8 x 9/16 (Fy = 36 ksi, w/t = 12.1 < (w/t)_lim = 13.3, rz = 1.59 in., A = 8.68 in.^2): For L = 121 in. (L/rz = 76), Fa = 29.5 ksi, Design strength = 256 kip. For L = 238 in. (L/rz = 150), Fa = 12.7 ksi, Design strength = 110 kip.
2. L6 x 6 x 5/16 (Fy = 36 ksi, w/t = 16.6 > (w/t)_lim = 13.3, Fcr = 30.0 ksi, rz = 1.20 in., A = 3.65 in.^2): For L = 180 in. (L/rz = 150), Fa = 12.7 ksi, Design strength = 46.4 kip.
3. L8 x 8 x 9/16 (Fy = 50 ksi, w/t = 12.1 > (w/t)_lim = 11.3, Fcr = 47.6 ksi): For L = 121 in. (L/rz = 76), Fa = 35.6 ksi, Design strength = 309 kip. For L = 238 in. (L/rz = 150), Fa = 12.7 ksi, Design strength = 110 kip.

clause_list.title: Example 2: Effect of End Connections on Member Capacity
clause_list.text:
Evaluates a compression strut L1-3/4 x 1-1/4 x 3/16 (rz = 0.27 in., A = 0.53 in.^2, Fy = 36 ksi) in a tension-only system:
- For L = 32 in. (L/rz = 119 <= 120): Eccentricity in critical axis at both ends [Eq. (3.7-7)] gives KL/r = 60 + 0.5(119) = 119.5; Fa = 19.8 ksi, Design strength = 10.5 kip.
- For L = 54 in. (L/rz = 200) with single-bolt connections (no restraint at ends, Eq. 3.7-8): KL/r = 200; Fa = 7.2 ksi, Design strength = 3.8 kip.
- For L = 54 in. (L/rz = 200) with multiple-bolt connections (partial restraint at both ends, Eq. 3.7-10): KL/r = 46.2 + 0.615(200) = 169.2; Fa = 10.0 ksi, Design strength = 5.3 kip.

clause_list.title: Example 3: Concentric Loading, Two-Angle Member
clause_list.text: Illustrates a back-to-back double-angle compression strut in a tension-only system where L/rx or L/ry is the critical factor under concentric loading: for L/r from 0 to 120, use Eq. (3.7-5); for L/r > 120, use Eq. (3.7-8) for single-bolt connections or Eq. (3.7-10) for multiple-bolt connections with partial restraint at both ends.

clause_list.title: Example 4: K-Bracing, Two-Angle Member with Varying Forces
clause_list.text:
Demonstrates in-plane (0.5 L / rx) and out-of-plane (L / ry) buckling checks for a K-braced horizontal strut not braced normal to the plane of the truss (Section 3.7.4.4):
1. Both subpanels in compression (P1 = -5.6 kip, P2 = -3.3 kip): Eq. (3.7-14a) gives K' = 0.75 + 0.25 * (3.3 / 5.6) = 0.90.
2. One subpanel in compression, one in tension (P1 = -44.6 kip, P2 = +2.2 kip): Eq. (3.7-14b) gives K' = 0.75 - 0.25 * (2.2 / 44.6) = 0.74.
3. With normal framing eccentricity at both ends (L = 9.0 ft, ry = 1.38 in.): L' = K' * L = 0.74 * 9.0 = 6.66 ft; L'/ry = 57.9; Eq. (3.7-7) gives KL'/ry = 60 + 0.5(57.9) = 89.

clause_list.title: Example 5: Effect of Subdivided Panels and End Connections
clause_list.text: Evaluates a single-angle compression strut (L1-3/4 x 1-1/4 x 3/16, rz = 0.27 in., ry = 0.37 in., A = 0.53 in.^2, Fy = 36 ksi) braced at mid-length in one plane (0.5 L / rz or L / ry critical), comparing capacities for L = 44 in. (L/ry = 119, P = 10.5 kip) and L = 74 in. (L/ry = 200) with single-bolt ends (3.8 kip) vs. multiple-bolt ends (5.3 kip).

clause_list.title: Example 6: Concentric Loading, Two-Angle Member, Subdivided Panels
clause_list.text: Defines the governing slenderness rules (0.5 L / rx or L / ry) for a concentrically loaded two-angle compression strut with a mid-panel intermediate brace under single-bolt vs. multiple-bolt end connections.

clause_list.title: Example 7: X-Brace Systems with No Intermediate Redundant Supports
clause_list.text:
Specifies the governing in-plane and out-of-plane slenderness factors for tension/compression X-brace diagonals connected at the crossover point:
1. When the tension diagonal has a force >= 20% of the compression diagonal force, the crossover point provides support resisting out-of-plane buckling (critical factor L1/rz or L1/rx,y).
2. When the tension diagonal has a force < 20% of the compression diagonal force (or if both diagonals are in compression), the crossover point does not provide out-of-plane support (critical out-of-plane factor L3/rx,y over full diagonal length L3, or (L1 + 0.5 L2)/ry when unequal legs are used with the long leg connected).

clause_list.title: Example 8: X-Brace Systems with Intermediate Redundant Supports — Case 1
clause_list.text: Specifies governing slenderness factors (L1/rz, L2/rz, L1/rx,y, or L3/rx,y) and applicable KL/r equations for X-brace diagonals with intermediate redundant bracing when the tension diagonal force is >= 20% vs. < 20% of the compression diagonal force. No rotational end restraint is assumed in the segment between the crossover point and the intermediate redundant support point.

clause_list.title: Example 9: X-Brace Systems with Intermediate Redundant Supports — Case 2
clause_list.text: Specifies governing slenderness factors for X-brace diagonals with alternate intermediate redundant bracing geometry (L1 > L2 and L1 > L4) when the tension diagonal force is >= 20% vs. < 20% of the compression diagonal force.

clause_list.title: Example 10: Cold-Formed Angle
clause_list.text:
Calculates the compression capacity of a 60-degree/90-degree cold-formed angle (Fy = 50 ksi, t = 0.135 in., w = 2.6775 in., w/t = 19.8, rz = 0.586 in., A = 0.777 in.^2):
- Local buckling: (w/t)_lim = 80 / sqrt(50) = 11.3; 144 / sqrt(50) = 20.4. Since 11.3 < 19.8 < 20.4, Eq. (3.7-2) gives Fcr = [1.677 - 0.677 * (19.8 / 11.3)] * 50 = 24.6 ksi, and Cc = pi * sqrt(2 * 29,000 / 24.6) = 152.5.
- At L = 117 in. (L/rz = 200 > Cc): Single-bolt connection [Eq. (3.7-8)] gives P = 5.6 kip; two-bolt connection [Eq. (3.7-10), KL/r = 169.2] gives P = 7.8 kip.
- At L = 58.5 in. (L/rz = 100 < Cc): Two-bolt connection with eccentricities at both ends [Eq. (3.7-7), KL/r = 110] gives Fa = 18.2 ksi and P = 14.1 kip.

clause_list.title: Example 11: Cold-Formed Lipped Angle
clause_list.text:
Calculates the compression capacity of a symmetrical cold-formed 3 in. x 3 in. x 0.135 in. lipped angle (Fy = 50 ksi, Cc = 106.9, A = 1.03 in.^2, w/t = 2.33 / 0.135 = 17.3, Cw = 0.441 in.^6, J = 0.00623 in.^4, Ips = 5.18 in.^4, rps = 2.24 in., ru = 1.32 in., rz = 0.773 in., uo = 1.64 in., L = 90 in.):
- Minimum lip depth [Eq. (3.8-3) with theta = 90 deg]: d_min = 0.93 in. <= actual lip depth.
- Equivalent radius of gyration [Eqs. (3.8-2) and (3.8-1)]: rt = 0.689 in., rtf = 0.639 in. < rz = 0.773 in., so torsional-flexural buckling governs (L/rtf = 90 / 0.639 = 141).
- With two-bolt connections [Eq. (3.7-10)]: KL/rtf = 46.2 + 0.615(141) = 133 > Cc; Fa = 16.2 ksi; Design strength = 16.2 * 1.03 = 16.7 kip.

clause_list.title: Example 12: M-Section as Column Member
clause_list.text:
Evaluates an M4 x 13 wide-flange column (Fy = 50 ksi, A = 3.81 in.^2, rx = 1.66 in., ry = 0.939 in., Sx = 5.24 in.^3, Cw = 11.06 in.^6, J = 0.19 in.^4, L = 96 in.):
1. Concentrically loaded (Section 3.9.4): Torsional buckling rt = 1.56 in. > ry = 0.939 in., so weak-axis flexural buckling governs (L/ry = 102.2 < Cc = 106.9). Fa = 27.15 ksi, Design strength Pa = 103.4 kip.
2. Connected on one flange at each end (2.0 in. eccentricity, P = 50 kip): Checked as a beam-column per Section 3.12 [Eq. (3.12-1)]. Lateral-torsional buckling [Eq. (3.14-1)] gives Fb = 43.6 ksi and Max = 228.5 in.-kip. Interaction ratio = 0.484 + 0.515 = 0.999 < 1.0 (acceptable for 50 kip; demonstrates the large capacity reduction caused by end eccentricity).

clause_list.title: Example 13: Channel as Column
clause_list.text:
Evaluates a cold-formed channel column (6 in. x 1.5 in. x 0.12 in., Fy = 36 ksi, A = 1.02 in.^2, rx = 2.06 in., ry = 0.48 in., L = 48 in.):
1. Concentrically loaded (Section 3.9.5): Torsional-flexural rtf = 0.847 in. > ry = 0.48 in., so y-axis flexural buckling governs (L/ry = 100 < Cc = 126). Fa = 24.7 ksi; flange and web w/t are fully effective per Section 3.9.3.1; Design strength Pa = 25.2 kip.
2. Connected to back of web (eccentricity e = 0.41 in. about y-axis): Interaction Eq. (3.12-1) gives a design strength of 8.7 kip (0.35 + 0.64 = 0.99 < 1.0).

clause_list.title: Example 14: T-Section as Column
clause_list.text:
Evaluates a concentrically loaded T-section column (Fy = 50 ksi, A = 2.775 in.^2, rx = 1.491 in., ry = 1.504 in., L = 120 in.):
- Torsional-flexural buckling [Eqs. (3.8-2) and (3.8-1) with y-axis as axis of symmetry] gives rt = 1.41 in. and rtf = 1.19 in. < rx, ry. Thus L/rtf = 120 / 1.19 = 100.8 < Cc = 106.9, and Fa = 27.7 ksi.
- Stem element w/t = 13.96 > 72 / sqrt(27.7) = 13.68 [Eq. (3.9-1)], so effective width b reduces the cross-sectional area from 2.775 in.^2 to 2.755 in.^2. Design strength = 27.7 * 2.755 = 76.3 kip.

clause_list.title: Example 15: Schifflerized Angle with Symmetrical Bracing
clause_list.text:
Evaluates an L8 x 8 x 1/2 hot-rolled angle that has had its legs closed to 60 degrees (Schifflerized angle) with symmetrical bracing (L = 9.0 ft = 108 in., Fy = 36 ksi, A = 7.75 in.^2, ru = 2.40 in., rz = 1.83 in., rps = 3.58 in., J = 0.646 in.^4, Cw = 3.68 in.^6, Ips = 172 in.^4):
- Per Sections 3.7 and 3.9.5, checked for flexural buckling about u- and z-axes and torsional-flexural buckling about the u-axis.
- Eqs. (3.8-2) and (3.8-1) give rt = 1.33 in. and rtf = 1.216 in., so KL/rtf = 108 / 1.216 = 88.8 governs over KL/ru = 45.0 and KL/rz = 59.0.
- Local buckling: w/t = 13.75 > (w/t)_lim = 13.3, giving Fcr = 35.2 ksi and Cc = 127.5. From Eq. (3.6-1), Fa = 26.7 ksi and Design strength = 26.7 * 7.75 = 206.9 kip.

clause_list.title: Example 16: Schifflerized Angle with Unsymmetrical Bracing
clause_list.text:
Evaluates a 60-degree Schifflerized angle L6 x 6 x 3/8 used as the lower chord of a triangular tower bridge with staggered panel points (L = 9.0 ft = 108 in., warping length = L/2 = 54 in., Ku = 0.5, Kz = 0.866, Fy = 36 ksi, A = 4.36 in.^2, ru = 1.84 in., rz = 1.44 in.):
- Using mixed end conditions (Section C3.8), K' * L / rtf = 94.8 governs. Adjusting for normal framing eccentricities at both ends [Eq. (3.7-7)] gives KL/rtf = 60 + 0.5(94.8) = 107.4.
- With w/t = 13.7 > 13.3, Fcr = 35.3 ksi, Cc = 127.3, Fa = 22.7 ksi, and Design strength = 22.7 * 4.36 = 99.0 kip.

clause_list.title: Example 17: j-Value Determination for Singly Symmetric Open Section
clause_list.text:
Demonstrates the analytical evaluation of Eq. (3.14-4) to determine the monosymmetry section property j for a cold-formed channel (8 in. web x 2 in. flanges x 0.135 in. thick, Iy = 0.485 in.^4, shear center coordinate xo = -0.922 in.) bent about the axis perpendicular to its axis of symmetry (Section 3.14.7):
- Dividing the channel into two flange rectangles (Areas 1 and 3) and one web rectangle (Area 2), the closed-form integral of (x^2 + y^2) * x * dA evaluates to 2.8533 - 1.9137 + 2.8533 = 3.79 in.^5.
- Substituting into Eq. (3.14-4): j = [1 / (2 * 0.485)] * (3.79) - (-0.922) = 4.83 in.

clause_list.title: Appendix C: Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text: Appendix C provides nonbinding engineering guidelines for evaluating, upgrading, or uprating existing latticed steel transmission towers designed prior to current ASCE standards.

clause_list.title: Introduction (Upgrading and Uprating Existing Towers)
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text: When utilities upgrade or uprate transmission lines (modifying conductors or shield wires), existing towers designed before current ASCE standards may not meet every current provision without extensive changes. Historic service performance, past full-scale test results, and potential degradation from aging/corrosion (especially in coastal or harsh industrial environments) should all be evaluated.

clause_list.title: Slenderness Ratios in Existing Towers
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text: Existing towers may have members exceeding the slenderness limits of Section 3.4. If the member capacity determined by this Standard (without limitation to the L/r ranges) meets or exceeds the new member force, and there is no history of wind-vibration fatigue failures, it may not be necessary to modify the existing member solely to meet current L/r limits. Any new or replacement members added to the existing tower should meet the requirements of the Standard.

clause_list.title: Minimum Distances in Existing Connections
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text: If existing tower members do not satisfy the minimum end distance, bolt spacing, or edge distance recommendations of Section 4.5, engineering judgment or sample connection testing should be used to verify capacity under the new loading condition. Replacement members should meet current Section 4.5 criteria.

clause_list.title: Bolt Shear Capacity & Field Sampling (ASTM F606)
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text: When bolt shear capacities are unknown on older towers, a random sample of bolts should be removed and tested per ASTM F606 (2013). A minimum of 1 bolt for every 10,000 bolts of like diameter and manufacturer is suggested, with a minimum of 10 bolts and a reasonable upper limit of 100 bolts for long lines. Testing should be completed with threads in the shear plane unless existing tower details (such as washers or recessed nuts) eliminate this possibility.

clause_list.title: Bearing Capacity of Bolts and Members
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text: Older tower designs often did not check bearing stress. For modern ASTM A394 Type 0 (Fu = 74 ksi) and Type 1 or A325 bolts (Fu = 120 ksi up to 1 in. diameter) connecting A36 (Fu = 58 ksi) or A572-50 (Fu = 65 ksi) steel, member Fu governs bearing capacity. On older towers, however, bearing capacity may be governed by the bolt material.

clause_list.title: Tested Towers
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text: Per Sections 3.18 and 3.7.4.6, original full-scale proof test data or component/connection test results from existing towers can be used to substantiate modified KL/r values or connection capacities during an upgrade or uprate.

clause_list.title: Member Use Ratios
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text: When analyzing older towers with modern 3D computer methods, calculated member forces may exceed design capacities. While overstressed members often require reinforcement (additional bracing, bolts, or member replacement), in some cases it may be acceptable for member use ratios to slightly exceed 100% of capacity for nonlegislated extreme event load cases, provided the owner is informed of the associated risk.

clause_list.title: Man-Load on Horizontal Members
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text: OSHA and ASCE MOP 74 climbing load criteria may not be met by horizontal members on older towers. The owner should be notified of these limitations and alternate tower maintenance/climbing procedures should be considered.

clause_list.title: Minimum Support of Redundant Members
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text: Redundant members in older towers were normally designed only to meet L/r limits without calculating the 1.5% to 2.5% bracing force Pr of Section 3.16. New redundant members added during an upgrade should meet Section 3.16, but it is not reasonable to replace an entire existing redundant system that has performed satisfactorily in service solely to meet the new Section 3.16 force criterion.

clause_list.title: Bars Used as Tension Hangers in Cross Arms
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text: Older towers frequently used solid square, rectangular, or round bar stock as tension-only cross-arm hangers or X-brace diagonals with very high slenderness ratios (L/r >> 500). High L/r bars can vibrate under low, steady wind conditions and develop fatigue cracks at bolt holes. If historic maintenance records indicate fatigue failures, replacement members should meet current slenderness criteria (Section 3.4); if no failures have occurred, site conditions likely do not induce damaging fatigue.

clause_list.title: ASTM and CSA Material Specifications Used in Older Towers
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text:
When original steel specifications are unknown on older towers, the following historical timeline applies (see Table C.11-1):
- Pre-1960 (U.S.): Likely ASTM A7 steel (combined A7-36 and A9-36 in 1937; Fu = 60–72 ksi, Fy = 0.5 Fu >= 33 ksi).
- 1960–1970 (U.S.): Either ASTM A7 (last listed as A7-61T) or ASTM A36 (first published as A36-60T in 1960; Fy = 36 ksi, Fu = 58–80 ksi). High-strength steels introduced in AISC 6th Ed. (1963) included ASTM A242, A440, A373-58T, and A441.
- Post-1970 (U.S.): Minimum of ASTM A36 steel, plus ASTM A572 (introduced in ASTM in 1966, AISC 8th Ed. in 1980) and ASTM A588 (introduced in ASTM in 1968, AISC 7th Ed. in 1970).
- Canada (1964–Present): CSA introduced G40.12 steel in 1964 (Fu = 62 ksi, Fy = 44 ksi for angles < 3/4 in. thick, 40 ksi for thicker angles). Canadian suppliers currently use CSA G40.21 44W (300W) steel in lieu of A36 (Fu = 65–90 ksi, Fy = 44 ksi).

clause_list.title: Original Compression Formulas Used in Older Tower Designs
clause_list.section: Appendix C — Guidelines for Existing Towers
clause_list.text: Before the first edition of the ASCE Guide for Design of Steel Transmission Towers (Manual 52, 1971), designers used company-specific straight-line compression formulas without effective length K-factors, block shear checks, or bearing checks. Consequently, evaluating an older tower leg with ASCE 10-15 (K = 1) often yields a higher capacity in the low L/r range than the original straight-line formula, whereas evaluating a strut that is eccentric at both ends (Curve 3, Eq. 3.7-7) may yield a smaller capacity than the original formula due to the K-factor.
